title: Code-Switching Between English and Spanish: Why It’s OK
seo_title: Code-Switching Between English and Spanish: Why It’s OK
meta_description: Code switching between English and Spanish is natural, skilled and common. What it is, why bilinguals do it, and what Spanglish says about language.
excerpt: Mixing English and Spanish isn’t a sign of confusion. It’s a skill bilingual people use every day.

body_html:
Code switching is what happens when a bilingual person moves between two languages in the same conversation, sometimes in the same sentence: “I was going to call you, pero se me olvidó.” For years, people treated this mixing between English and Spanish as a sign that someone didn’t know either language well. Linguists now see it very differently. Code switching is a skilled, rule-governed and deeply human way of speaking.

Key takeaways
  • Code switching is normal among bilinguals and follows grammatical patterns.
  • People switch for emotion, emphasis, identity, humour or simply the best word.
  • Spanglish is a real way of speaking with its own history and creativity.
  • For learners, mixing languages early on is a bridge, not a failure.
{{toc}}

What is code switching?

Code-switching is the alternating use of two or more languages in conversation. It can happen between sentences (“I’m tired. Vámonos a casa.”) or inside a sentence (“Let’s get un cafecito before work.”).

One of the most famous studies of English–Spanish code switching was published by linguist Shana Poplack in 1980, with the memorable title “Sometimes I’ll start a sentence in Spanish y termino en español.” Studying Puerto Rican speakers in New York, she found that switching tends to happen at points where the grammar of both languages fits together. In other words, fluent bilinguals switch smoothly, not randomly.

Why bilinguals switch between English and Spanish

  • The perfect word. Some ideas just feel better in one language. Sobremesa or antojo say in one word what English needs a sentence for. I gathered more in {{link:spanish-words-with-no-english-translation|Spanish words with no English translation}}.
  • Emotion. Many people express affection, anger or prayer in the language they grew up with.
  • Emphasis and humour. Repeating something in the other language can make a point stronger or funnier.
  • Identity. Switching can signal belonging to a family, community or culture.
  • Audience. People naturally adjust to whoever is listening: Spanish with grandma, English with a colleague, both with siblings.
{{image:2}}

Is Spanglish “real” language?

Spanglish is a broad term for the mixing of English and Spanish, especially in the United States. It includes code switching and also borrowed words adapted to Spanish, such as parquear (to park) or lonche (lunch). Some people dismiss it as “bad Spanish”, but linguists generally describe it as a natural result of two languages living side by side, much like the many English words borrowed from French centuries ago.

That doesn’t mean every situation calls for it. In a formal letter or an exam, you will usually choose one language. The point is that mixing is a choice skilled bilinguals make, not a lack of ability.

{{book:a-road-in-bloom}}

Code switching for learners

If you are learning Spanish, you have probably dropped an English word into a Spanish sentence when you got stuck: “Quiero comprar un… blender.” That is fine. It keeps the conversation going and shows exactly which word you need to learn next. Ask “¿Cómo se dice blender?” and you will hear licuadora, a word you are likely to remember because you needed it.

Some bilingual books even use this mixing on purpose, weaving Spanish phrases into English sentences so learners absorb them naturally. I compare formats in {{link:bilingual-books-english-spanish|how to use English–Spanish bilingual books}}.

Code switching in families

Children growing up with English and Spanish often mix languages, especially when one is stronger. Parents sometimes worry this means confusion, but it is a normal stage of bilingual development. Over time, children learn which language to use with whom. I share practical ideas in {{link:raising-bilingual-children-english-spanish|raising bilingual children in English and Spanish}}.

For adults who grew up with Spanish at home but answer in English, code switching can be a comfortable way back into the family language. If that sounds familiar, {{link:heritage-spanish-speakers|my guide for heritage Spanish speakers}} is for you.

{{image:3}}

Common examples of English–Spanish switching

ExampleWhy the switch happens
“I’m so tired, ay, qué día.”Emotion feels more natural in Spanish
“Mi jefe wants the report by Friday.”Habit: the word that comes to mind first
“Te quiero mucho, okay? Drive safe.”Affection in the family language
“Vamos al mall después.”A borrowed word everyone in the community uses

Code switching is part of what makes bilingual life rich. For the full picture of learning and living between the two languages, see my complete guide to {{link:bilingual-english-and-spanish|bilingual English and Spanish}}.

When to choose one language

Code switching is natural, but context still matters. In a job interview, a formal email or a classroom exercise, it usually makes sense to stay in one language. For learners, it can also help to set short “Spanish only” periods, such as ten minutes at dinner, to stretch yourself. The goal is not to stop mixing forever. It is to be able to choose: switching when it adds warmth or precision, and staying in one language when the moment calls for it.

How to talk about code switching with others

If someone criticizes the way you or your family mix English and Spanish, it can help to know that linguists have studied this for decades and consistently describe it as a sign of bilingual skill. You can also explain your reasons: some words simply feel truer in one language, and switching lets you speak to everyone in the room. Pride in both languages, and in the way they meet in your voice, is entirely justified.

Final thoughts

Mixing English and Spanish is not a flaw to fix. It is a sign of a mind that holds two languages and chooses between them, moment by moment. Learners can use it as a bridge, families as a comfort and communities as a voice of their own.

faq.q: What is code switching in English and Spanish?
faq.a: It is moving between English and Spanish within one conversation or even one sentence. It is common among bilingual speakers and follows grammatical patterns.

faq.q: Is code switching bad for learning Spanish?
faq.a: No. For learners it keeps conversations going and highlights the words you still need. Over time you will need English less and less.

faq.q: Is Spanglish the same as code switching?
faq.a: Spanglish is a broader term that includes code switching and English words adapted into Spanish, such as parquear for “to park”.
